title: The World Is Held Together by Duct Tape?  Intel's Failed Bitcoin Chip Bet
author: M
text:
D

DanX
Active member

The World Is Held Together by Duct Tape: Intel's Failed Bitcoin Chip Bet​
I never understood Intel's bitcoin mining chip from start to finish. In 2022 they spent more than $100 million on it, and in the end there was nothing to show for it. Other than "the world is held together by duct tape," I can't come up with any explanation.

When they entered, I was nervous​
When we built our BTC chips, much of our thinking on dynamic logic came from the experience Intel had built up designing CPUs. So when I heard Intel was going to make mining chips, I was genuinely worried. Intel's depth in dynamic logic far exceeds ours, and quite a few of its engineers have very distinctive techniques that a new company couldn't catch up with in a short time.

Then the product came out, and I was stunned: they didn't use dynamic logic.

A mining chip is judged on a single number: how many joules it burns per TH of hash rate. Officially, the Blockscale that Intel launched in April 2022 typically runs at about 35 J/TH, and at its best gets down to 26 J/TH. Bitmain was already at 20 J/TH by then. That means a cost at least twice as high. So what advantage did Intel have in doing this? I thought about it for a long time and couldn't find one.

My guess: using BTC to tune the process​
Later I saw Intel going all out on its new process nodes, using EUV to try to catch up with TSMC. So I guessed that maybe they were doing BTC to tune the process.

That guess makes sense. A mining chip is highly repetitive and can tolerate lower yield, because you can simply disable the cores that fail. Hash rate also converts directly into yield, so the feedback is fast. Even at low yield you can still sell the chips, which gives you a ready-made business model.

There is precedent. When SMIC was developing its 7 nm process, a mining chip was running on it, according to TechInsights' teardown. The chip is called MinerVa, and as far as I know it came from the same people as Canaan. The role of mining chips there was to help the new process work out its yield, and Canaan at least contributed on that point.

Then, in the second year, they stopped​
Intel launched the second-generation Blockscale in April 2022. In April 2023, an Intel spokesperson confirmed the product line had reached end-of-life. Support for existing customers would continue, and Intel said it would "continue to monitor market opportunities."

One year. During the same period, Intel was announcing a large round of cost cuts, with plans to save $3 billion in 2023.

If the mining chip was meant to tune the process, you wouldn't kill it at the second version, because tuning a process needs a continuous flow of orders, and a single trial run can't give you enough data. If it was meant to make money, you wouldn't pick an approach that doesn't use your own biggest strength. Neither explanation fits. That leaves one: this was a project nobody was really in charge of.

That last point is my guess, but I can't think of anything else.

At first, I thought Intel had strategic vision in BTC​
A plan that could use BTC to improve yield, and at the same time find a way out for the new process. Looking back now, I was wrong.

A company's most valuable resources are its process technology and its people. Intel had both, yet it took the most careless approach and built the shortest-lived product. I still don't understand what that $100-plus million actually bought.

Other than "the world is held together by duct tape," I can't think of any way to explain it?
